segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: A few years back, I gave a talk at Chautauqua, in upstate New York, which, if you don't know what that is, starting in the 1870s, it was this high-minded lecture circuit, like TED Talks, but before the internet or Public Radio before the invention of radio. With a big religious component, which is how I fell into this long conversation about the literal word of the Bible.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It happened because the staffer who drove me to the airport was a retired Methodist preacher and associate pastor of one of the churches in Chautauqua, named John Jackson. And we had this hour and a half long drive.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And somehow, we got onto how he doesn't believe that every word of the Bible is literally true, which, if you're a Methodist, that's no big deal. And John said, that as he gets older, the literal words of the Bible seem less important to him than the big picture-- love your neighbor as yourself, and love God above all.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And I told John, I totally get the "love your neighbor as yourself" part of that. I can see how that can reshape just everything about how you treat others and really everything you do in your life in the world.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But I told him, like, I've never really understood, why is it important to love God above all? Do you know what I mean? If you do what God wants, and you try to be good-- you try to treat others right-- what difference does it make if you love God? What does God care?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And I got to ask John about a variation on this question, that I've wondered about for a couple of years, ever since the last time I was in synagogue. This was, I don't know, this was two or three years before this conversation. I hadn't been to synagogue in forever.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And it was the anniversary of my mom's death. And we're Jews, so you're supposed to go say Kaddish, this old prayer that's one of the central prayers in Judaism, at the anniversary of somebody's death. And so my dad and my stepmom and I were at one of the daily services that observant Jews go to every day in Baltimore, where I grew up.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And I always liked going to synagogue as a kid. We went a lot. And so it was nice going back. I know all the Hebrew prayers by heart. And I don't know if this is good or bad, but not having sat in a synagogue in over a decade, it really hit me how every day is a rerun. Do you know what I mean? They never do a new episode-- every day, the same words, same songs, in the same order, stretching back hundreds of years. They read a new part of the Bible, part of the Torah, some days, so there's that. But all the rest-- basically exactly the same every day.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And everybody is singing and chanting. And I started looking in the prayer book on the side of the page with the English translation of the prayers, which I hadn't done in years. And I really was struck at how many of them-- the Amidah, the Ashrei, are about praising God at length. That's what the words mean, even the Kaddish, which you say over and over during services.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [SPEAKING HEBREW]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It goes on and on. And the words basically are, may His great name be exalted and sanctified, blessed and praised, glorified and exalted, extolled and honored, adored and lauded, be the name of the Holy One. And that is what they have say when your mom dies-- comforting, huh? It's basically God is great, over and over, building to this beautiful line, really beautiful, that's basically: God is so great, it's beyond the power of any prayer or word or song or praise. It's beyond the power of language to capture it.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And it really hit me, sitting there. What does God get out of that? Why does he want us sitting down and telling him how great he is for 45 minutes a day? Is he that needy? If some parent demanded that of their kids-- OK, I want you to praise me for 45 minutes a day, every single day of your life, we would know they were nuts.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And it's like what I was saying to John-- what does God care if we love him? And John had such a lovely answer. He said, first off, he thinks lots of people make the mistake of picturing God as being like us, like humans, like he's somebody who we're calling on the phone, or something, when we're praying. But the way he sees it, he understands God to be all the values and principles that he sees in scripture-- the obligation to love each other, to be honest and decent in our dealings with each other, all of those things.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And when he's praising God, he said, that's what he's praising. He's basically re-pledging himself to those principles, which he loves. In other words, the literal words of the Bible, the literal words of the prayers, aren't as important as that pledge, a pledge to act a certain way in the world.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And reading and calling around in the days since we had that conversation, I've learned that other clergy-- Christian, Jewish, Muslim-- some of them say the same things, especially that God doesn't need our prayers. The prayers are for us. One of them told me the Kaddish is supposed to comfort me after my mom's death by pointing me to this idea of God's presence in the world, the goodness in the world, which, if I believed in God, I guess could be a comfort.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But I don't believe. But weirdly, even without that, without believing any of the words, I do find it's a comfort to say the prayer. It's just it's familiar. It's familiar as the nursery rhymes my mom sang to me as a kid, as the Shema, the prayer that she had me and my sister say every night before we went to sleep. It's comforting, despite the fact that it's in another language and part of a doctrine I don't believe anymore.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Just the fact of it handed to me by my parents and to them by their parents-- Freida and Lou and Melvin and Molly; and their parents before them-- David, Elizabeth, and Isidore; and people whose names I don't even know; and before them, their parents for hundreds and hundreds and hundreds of years; and standing in synagogue that day, standing and saying these words in unison with other mourners, it was comforting.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [SPEAKING HEBREW]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Today on our show, the sometimes very old words that we turn to for comfort in moments of adversity and at other times, they can be very random-- the novel Little Women, A Tribe Called Quest and other old school hip hop-- we have stories about each of those. From WBEZ Chicago, it's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. Stay with us.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act 1-- Go to the Mattresses. Shamyla always loved books. Back in 1989, like lots of other 11-year-olds, she also loved Punky Brewster and Paula Abdul. But her main thing was reading-- The Baby-Sitters Club books, Little House on the Prairie. It was all about words and books.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And then something happened, which totally changed what she read and how. Elna Baker talked to her. This is a story we first broadcast a few years ago. Today's show is a rerun. Here's Elna.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: OK, so you meet somebody at a party, and they ask you, what's your favorite book? What's your answer?

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: My answer is Little Women is my all-time favorite book.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And then if they were to ask you, why? What would you say?

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: Well, I probably would have a very long conversation with someone about that. But it goes back to the '90s, when I was living in Pakistan. And this was the only book that I had in my possession for a couple of years.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: A couple of years, when she was basically held in captivity in Pakistan. I'll tell you how she found herself holed up with only one book in a minute. But first, here's how she ended up in captivity.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: She was raised in suburban Maryland. Her father was an economist, her mom a teacher. She went to an all-girls prep school. At 11, she learned her parents weren't her biological parents. Her mom, the oldest daughter in her family, couldn't have kids and really wanted to.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And so Shamyla's family came up with a solution, one that's not unusual in Pakistan. Since her mom was the oldest, it was her younger sister's obligation to give her a child. And because of this family pressure and a sense of duty, the younger sister did it. But then it got complicated.

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: Well, my adoptive parents had kids. They had a son. And then they had another son. And that really made my biological family confused and angry. And they were like, we gave you our child, and now you have your own children. Give us our daughter back.

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: And my mom said, I'm not going to give her back. She's not a ball. I can't toss her back.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: For years, they fought over this. When Shamyla was 12, on a visit home to Pakistan, her birth parents asked if they could take her on a trip. Her mom agreed, as a gesture of goodwill. It'd just be a week long, and she'd get to know her cousins, who were actually her brothers. And at first, it was really fun.

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: Until I got really sick at someone's house. And it turned out I had malaria. And what I didn't realize at the time was that they had taken me there on purpose, because it was way out in the country, where no one could find me.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Two weeks go by, then three. She's all better, asking when she can go back.

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: And they kept making excuses-- um, not-- you just need to wait. We have some other places to go. And I remember, at some point, my biological father taking me aside very kindly and saying, you know, we're your real family. They never loved you. We love you.

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: They loved you like the way people love slippers, like an old, used pair of slippers. But they love their boys, because that's their blood. And we're your blood, and that's how we love you. So you're staying with us now.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: They don't let her leave, and she's really confused-- of course, my US parents love me. They must love me. But then, if they loved me, why aren't they coming to get me?

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Unbeknownst to her, her US parents are trying to find out where she is. But no one will tell them. To make matters worse, her US parents are not legally Shamyla's parents. The adoption was never formal. She was just handed over. So they have no legal claim to their daughter, and there's nothing Shamyla could do. She was 12.

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: Even if I fantasized about running away to another city and seeing other relatives, I was like, how will I do it? What will I do? Where will I get the money? How will I get on the train? How will I get on a plane? What will I do?

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: You were trapped.

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: I was trapped, yeah.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: She says her birth parents told her, when she was growing up, whenever they saw her, it was upsetting to them. They thought, she's too Americanized. They were incredibly traditional, even for Pakistan, which is already very patriarchal. Women are expected to be subordinate. And if their purity is questioned, like if they're even seen speaking to a man in a public place, their family's reputation could be ruined, and the whole family could be ostracized from the community for it.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: This is especially the case in Peshawar, where her birth parents lived. And Shamyla, a suburban Maryland tween, didn't understand that this was the world she lived in now. She says everything about the way she acted was wrong in their eyes. They didn't approve of the music she listened to or the books she read. They thought they were teaching her to be far too independent for a girl.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: At this rate, she'd become promiscuous any day now. And since they didn't trust her not to be, they kept her under house arrest, confining her to a corner of the house that consisted of a bedroom and a bathroom. And they confiscated her cassettes and her books. Her birth father would lecture to her for hours.

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: His favorite three topics were America is a bad place, especially for girls. American women are loose character and horrible. The second topic was your adopted family never really loved you, never. And the third topic was, so here's what you're going to do when you get married. These are your wifely duties, including your sexual obligations to your husband.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: He'd also lecture her about the rules she needed to follow. Some were the normal rules of an observant Muslim home. She couldn't go out without being covered, make eye contact, wear her hair down. Others were cultural-- she couldn't hug people; wear glasses when guests came over; speak English or Urdu, which would be seen as a sign of modernity. Only Pashto, the language of the region, was allowed.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: She couldn't serve herself food before her brothers. She was barely allowed to eat. They thought she needed to be thin to get married, so they locked the fridge. She says, if she messed up, she was beaten with a kitchen squeegee, which cut her face open, or a walking stick. That was the worst one, she says.

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: The second worst one was with a golf club. And the third worst one was with cleats near my eye.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: They took cleats and hit you with them.

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: And I think I got kicked.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: She asked me not to reach out to her birth parents to confirm these details, because she was worried for her safety. And I didn't. But members of her family here in the States confirmed that this is what her birth parents are like. And her mother and therapist corroborated that her story of being abused has always remained consistent.

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: I remember, after every time they would beat me, I'd put an X on whatever calendar I had and be like, this will never happen again. I will be so good now, that this will never happen again.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Like, from this day forward, I'll finally be a good girl.

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: Yep.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Did you feel like you'd never be the girl they wanted you to be?

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: No, I thought eventually, I'm going to get there. I just have to keep trying. I really thought that eventually, I'm going to become that person.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And you wanted to be that person?

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: I think that I thought I had no choice.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: She wasn't just physically abused. As she got older, she says, she was also sexually abused by her brother. And finally, into this bleakness, comes a book, the book, Little Women.

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: So one of my friends noticed the book at a book fair at our school. All these books had come from Singapore. And there was Little Women. I said, I know this book, and I want it. And I remember thinking, oh my god, I read that book when I was little. I had a huge, beautiful illustrated copy growing up. And I said to my friend Mirjana, I was like, Mirjana, can you please buy it? It's 10 rupees, and I'll pay you back.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: She'd tried smuggling books home before, but she'd always been caught. She hid the book inside her mattress pad underneath the bed. And she broke it into sections, roughly eight piles, so that it didn't make the mattress stick up in any way.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: When she heard her family go out, she'd wait, and then carefully unzip the mattress pad, and take a section of the book out at a time. Whichever one she pulled out first, she read.

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: It was the book of my life. It was the only book I had to escape. It was the only book that I had to actually read over and over again. And I kind of memorized it.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: I'm going to read you like some quotes from the book.

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And just interrupt if you know where it is or what this is about. And then I'm going to just random open book.

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: [CHUCKLING] This feels like a pop quiz.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Yeah, yeah. Ooh: Mercy on me. Beth loves Laurie, she said, sitting down in--

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: Oh, this is when Beth is ill. And Beth is changing, and she thinks the secret is that Beth is in love with Laurie.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Mrs. March and Jo were deep in their own affairs, when a sound from Meg made them look up to see her staring at her note.

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: Oh, that's when-- [LAUGHING] that's when Meg has written to Mr. Brooke, and he actually writes back. But it was Laurie pretending to be Mr. Brooke.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: We did this eight times, and she's able to get everything I read within seconds.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: You're good at this.

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: [LAUGHING] I told you, I read this book over and over and over.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: How many times?

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: Oh, hundreds. By now, it's probably thousands.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: If you haven't read Little Women, it's basically about four sisters, the March sisters. Meg, the oldest, is the responsible one. Jo is the rebel and the writer. Beth is sick. And Amy, the youngest, is a spoiled brat. Their father is serving in the Civil War, and their mother is raising them alone. The book follows these girls from childhood into adulthood.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Were there parts of the book that you would just read over and over, like, your favorite parts?

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: I loved reading the parts in the beginning, when the two sisters would talk to each other, Meg and Jo, and their bond. Because I didn't have a sister, and I had no one to talk to. And I really loved the scenes about parties and stuff.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: She loved these scenes, because they mirrored her life in a really specific way. Her birth parents were upper middle class, and they wanted to use Shamyla to marry into a higher class. So they dressed her up and took her to social events to show her off. In the book, there are events like this that the March sisters go to.

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: There's a chapter about Meg and Jo going to a party in the very beginning. And they're not out yet in society. And I was like, Oh my god, this 1860-something book is what's happening in Peshawar in 1990. Oh my god, it's the same thing. I'm not out yet in society, and I have to be very careful how I present myself.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: In a way, Little Women was the perfect book for Shamyla's situation, because it's like a how-to for girls, a survival guide. Like most women who read the book, the sister Shamyla relates to the most is Jo. She was my favorite, too.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: I was raised in a strict religion, and my life was supposed to be about marriage and motherhood. And then Jo came into my orbit and showed me I could have ambition, and be improper, and break the rules. And I loved her for it. And that's how Shamyla felt. Jo helped Shamyla hold on to the identity her family was trying so hard to squash.

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: There's a part where Jo and Laurie go running. And Meg scolds her and says, when will you learn to be ladylike? And she says, I hope never. I always want to run, and I always want to romp. And I thought, me too. I never want to have to stop being spirited and independent.

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: And I remember Jo had a temper in the book. And I thought, I have a temper, too. And she's working really hard to curb it, and I was like, I am, too. I didn't have any of the freedom Jo had. But in my heart, I was just as feisty and independent.

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: So I think it's very funny when nowadays, my friends are like, well, you were so meek. And I was like, I was never meek. That's just a facade. [LAUGHING] I'm Jo. I get her.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: But in a way, what's so interesting is it's so literally like your way of being Jo was reading about Jo. That's where you actually got to be Jo.

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: Yeah, I couldn't really do anything else.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: In the book, Jo writes stories. Shamyla loved to write, too. But she says, the second year she was there, her birth father declared, girls aren't supposed to write, and took a notebook filled with her stories, and burned it in the backyard, and made her watch. In the book, Jo writes her stories alone in the attic. This gave Shamyla the idea to sneak into her bathroom with a fountain pen and paper and write.

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: And then I would wash all the ink off the paper, crumple up the wet paper, and throw it up the hole in the window mesh.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Wait, you would write the stories and then erase everything you'd written?

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: So there was a hose that attached from the tub to the sink. And so I would take that hose and wash all the ink off.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Down the drain of--

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: There was a floor drain, and I'd make sure that the floor drain was not blue with the blue ink [LAUGHING] and that there was no sign of ink that had fallen off the papers.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Shamyla knew how our family would react if they caught her writing or if they found her copy of Little Women and read any of it. Like, there's a boy in the book. His name is Laurie. He and Jo have an innocent flirtation. But Shamyla says, if her birth parents read that part, they'd think--

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: You don't go over to adolescent boy's house ever. There's no innocence in this. In real life, Jo and Laurie would be doing very bad things. This is not right.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Well, they're saying, in real life, Jo and Laurie would be getting it on?

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: Basically.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: I mean, that would have been a better book, right?

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: [LAUGHING]

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: I loved that. Oh my gosh I was like, in my fan fiction, I would write that.

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: That's so funny.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: After a year, Shamyla's American mother was allowed to visit her. Shamyla told her what was happening. Her American mother cried and begged for her extended family to intervene and send Shamyla back to the States. But it was useless. Shamyla felt abandoned and hopeless. So she gave in, did her best to make herself into the obedient Pashtun girl they wanted her to be. There's a scene in the book, one I hated, because it was so sad, that Shamyla read over and over again.

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: I reread Beth's dying a lot, because there was this sense of helplessness. And I really understood that in a way that a lot of people don't. Because I knew, when something's inevitable, and it's going to happen, they keep saying, the tide is going out, in the book. And I was like, yeah, when the tide goes out, you just have to go with it. You can't fight it. I understood that on a level I couldn't even explain. I just knew what that meant.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: It sounds like their world feels so real to you.

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: [LAUGHING] I know. It really does. I felt like I lived with them sometimes.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: What do you mean?

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: I felt like I was watching them, like I was the servant, or something, watching. I felt like I lived in the attic, and I could go downstairs and see them. They couldn't see me, but I could see them. And I would join the world. I would join in.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Her real world, of course was much darker. By the time she got to 17 or 18, she concluded that there's really only one way out to escape her family and maybe even have a happy life.

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: I was like, OK, so the way out is marriage. So I have to play this game to get married. And I started to actually kind of be like, OK, so in Little Women, you know how Meg goes to society dances, and wears her glove, and starts putting her hair up?

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: I was like, I can do this. I can do this to get the best possible way out. I was really thinking about how to create my life with someone else and what that would look like. And so I had stopped so much caring about going home or going back.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And marriage is actually what the second part of Little Women is about. The second half of the book is very different from the first. It covers domestic duties and how the girls let go of their wild ways to become good wives.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Shamyla, not a big fan of Part Two.

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: The book, the second book, I remember thinking, I don't like this part. I like going back to their childhood and reading that part again.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Oh, the second part is the worst.

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: I know. It's so, so, so sad.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: I think I'd really forgotten the message of the second half of the book. And it's kind of infuriating, when you realize how, in some ways, it feels almost like a propaganda for becoming the way you're supposed to be.

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: Yeah. I remember thinking, when Meg gets married, they have a whole chapter about how she loses her freedom. And I was like, Oh god, I don't want that to be my story when I get married. I understood a lot of that, because that was what was being asked of me at that time, to give up, give up, give up, in order to be a woman to live in the society and be married and have a family.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: A friend at Shamyla's school told her she had a brother that Shamyla could marry, who would treat her well. So she began corresponding with him via her friend. But her family found out. And they were terrified that their reputation was going to be destroyed by it. Girls do not communicate directly with boys.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And they did what lots of families might do. They pulled her out of school and quickly started arranging her marriage to a 30-year-old man. As part of their damage control, they decided to send Shamyla away for a few weeks.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: But their only relatives who weren't in Peshawar were in America. So they made arrangements to send her back. And while she was there, her birth father and mother wanted her to learn new skills that would add to her bride price, the money the groom's family would be expected to pay them.

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: He sent me with a whole list. He was like, you have to learn driving, shorthand, swimming. [LAUGHING]

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: It just seems like, after all the work they did to get you to stay, and also, their plans to marry you off, it just seems crazy that they would let you go back.

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: Well it's funny, because she even said something crazy. She's like, if they're going to do anything to fix your face-- because remember, they cut my face open-- she's like, ask them if they can put a mole down there, like Cindy Crawford. And so I was like, OK, let's add mole to the list of things that will happen. [LAUGHING]

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: They send her to stay with her US parents. Her birth father is so confident that Shamyla is one of them now, that she'll obediently return to Pakistan. He doesn't question letting her go. A female chaperone traveled with her.

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: So we walked onto the tarmac. I climbed up in the plane. And as the plane took off, I just started crying nonstop. Because I knew I wasn't coming back. I just knew. I didn't know how I knew it. I don't know why I knew it. And I'm watching Pakistan slip away, and I'm like, I'm not going back here. It's never happening.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And was it relief?

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: No. I was sad. I was really, really sad. And I was like, goodbye, life that I knew.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: At first, she had a hard time coming back to America. She was in total culture shock. She could hardly speak English. She didn't recognize her little brothers. The internet existed now. It was like she'd woken up from a coma.

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: I remember thinking, I still like big hair. And everyone's like, that ended in 1989. No one does that anymore. And I was like, but I like that. They're like, no, now we straighten our hair. And I was like, I don't like that. Well, you have to.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: She enrolled in community college. But she'd been so indoctrinated, it was hard for her to just switch it off. She'd see women in skirts and catch herself judging them.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: For the first few years, she was a mess. Trying to switch off the ideology was nearly impossible. She started to see a therapist, who helped her process the extent of what happened to her.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: There's something her mother said to me on the phone I can't stop thinking about. It's something she told her little sister once. Between you and me, we've ruined Shamyla's life.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: It's been 23 years since she returned. Her life actually diverged from the second half of Little Women, the part she didn't like. She didn't get married, and she's independent. She runs her own practice as a therapist and social worker. She specifically works with people who suffer from trauma, because she understands it so well herself. But sometimes, she still returns to Little Women.

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: Well, it comes up in different situations. I'll be like, OK, so-- the other day, I actually-- this is funny. My friend has twins. And she was telling me, like, god, I'm so tired, and they don't listen, and my husband is so busy. And I referred her to the chapter of Meg trying to discipline her twins. And I was like, read this. This will help you. [LAUGHING]

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Wait, are you constantly-- do your friends have a joke or, like, Oh, not another Little Women reference.

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: No, I think that they think it's funny that I like the book so much. But I don't think anyone really understands why.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Wait, so it's like your only frame of reference?

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: When she's having a hard time or making a decision, she asks the question, opens the book, and whatever passage she reads, it's her answer from the March sisters. And she also has this ritual.

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: So every year on my birthday, I find the corresponding age that I am for the chapter I am, and I read that.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: In other words, chapter 30, when she turned 30; chapter 31, when she turned 31.

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: To be like, so what is this life-- this year going to be about in my life? What's it telling me?

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: So it's almost like your magic eight ball?

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: Yeah, kind of. It's like my Bible.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: What did you turn this year?

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And what chapter?

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: Oh Amy-- it's called Learning to Forget. It's when Laurie's trying to forget Jo, and he starts falling in love with Amy.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And how do you think that's going to relate to this year of be--

segments.speaker: Shamyla
segments.text: Maybe this year, finally someone's going to fall in love with me, [LAUGHING] the right one, not all the wrong ones.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: There are 47 chapters in Little Women. In six years, she'll turn 48. And she doesn't know what she'll do. She says maybe she'll start from the beginning again. And whereas the book used to be a way of escaping her room in Pakistan, now it's a way of returning to that world she built alone in her room. It's as if the March sisters are all still living there, and she's the one who left them behind.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This is "This American Life." I'm Ira Glass. Each week on our show, of course, we choose a theme, bring you different kinds of stories on that theme. Today's show-- "The Weight of Words," stories about the words that people turn to for comfort or strength. We first aired this show in 2019. We've arrived at Act 2 of our show, Act 2-- Daddy Lessons.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So the most recent bit of serious parenting that my dad did with me-- and I say this, realizing that this really might be the very last life lesson he might give me; we are both getting up there in years-- was a protracted month-long campaign to switch from Excel to Quicken, to keep track of my personal finances. He felt very strongly about this. And I just want to say, yes, the numbers add up the same, no matter what software you use.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But Quicken, I mean, don't get my dad started. He's a retired CPA. He had already trained me to save all my receipts. Please, that's basic. And he went on with this at such length, that at some point, I realized, Oh, switching software was not a piece of friendly financial advice. This was actual parenting happening.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Not switching to Quicken meant an actual repudiation of him as a father. It would actually be a failure of parenthood. Parents try to shape who we are in their own image so often. They make sure their kids are exposed to whatever-- modern art, sports, nature, science, theater, whatever they love. They train them to be the world's greatest tennis player or golfer, that kind of thing.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: My friend Adam came up with a scheme like that.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This is Neil Drumming. His friend Adam is Adam Mansbach, a writer.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: Adam is a DJ, a record collector, and he wanted his daughter Vivien to love music the way he loved music, exactly the way he loved music.

segments.speaker: Adam Mansbach
segments.text: One of the things I feel like I got right about parenting is that I never played Viv any kids music. Because I understood that any song that you played a two-year-old, a three-year-old, might become their favorite song, and then you would have to listen to it 20 times a day. So I never played her anything I wasn't willing to listen to 20 times a day. So she, from a very young age, was listening to a lot of music I liked.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: Is that a thing that you got right about parenting? Or is that a thing that you just did for yourself?

segments.speaker: Adam Mansbach
segments.text: I mean, [LAUGHING] I mean, aren't the two synonymous really, Neil? I'm not sure what the difference is.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: Adam likes '80s and '90s hip hop perhaps more than me, which is saying a lot. Anyway, he fed Vivien a steady diet of classic material-- A Tribe Called Quest, Public Enemy, Run-DMC. Das EFX.

segments.speaker: Adam Mansbach
segments.text: There was probably a year, probably two years, where the Stetsasonic record In Full Gear got more play in our house than any other record. We may be the only household in North America that can say that, that in the year 2014, we listened to In Full Gear more than any other album.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: [LAUGHING] What is that record, '88?

segments.speaker: Adam Mansbach
segments.text: Yeah, it came out in '88.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: This exposure therapy approach to parenting has been known to fail. I grew up surrounded by beds that were always made. But if you walked into my apartment now, you'd see no evidence of that. In Adam's case, though, it worked. He noticed that by the time she was six years old, Vivien could rap along to any hip hop song you played her.

segments.speaker: Adam Mansbach
segments.text: She would memorize it, and she would be very much in the pocket and just not missing a beat. I remember one of the songs that we played a lot was The Choice is Yours," remixed by Black Sheep. I remember recording her just on my phone, doing the third verse of the song, the famous third verse of the song, Engine Engine Number 9.

segments.speaker: Vivien
segments.text: If my train goes off the track, pick it up, pick it up, pick it up. Back on the seat, crispy and clean. You can try, but know what--

segments.speaker: Adam Mansbach
segments.text: And she had it perfectly down. And it's not an easy verse to do. And I remember sending it to our friend Jay Period, who in turn sent it to Dres, from Black Sheep. And he was like, Yo, this is incredible. Like, tell her-- give her my props.

segments.speaker: Adam Mansbach
segments.text: And I was like, Yo, Viv, you're six, so this means nothing to you. But Dres from Black Sheep said that you're dope. This is his song.

segments.text: [MUSIC - "THE CHOICE IS YOURS" BY BLACK SHEEP]

segments.speaker: Adam Mansbach
segments.text: (RAPPING) Engine, engine number 9, on the New York transit line, if my train goes off the track, pick it up, pick it up, pick it up. Come on.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: Like a lot of guys our age, Adam tried his hand at being a rapper when he was younger. He joined a group. They made some songs that never quite went anywhere. He stayed in the hip hop world, though. He still has a lot of connections.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: So he was thrilled to find out his daughter had some skills. And proud father that he is, he wanted more people to know. When another one of his entertainment industry buddies needed a theme song for a PBS Kids show he was making, called "Bug Bites," Adam jumped at the chance to write Vivien some original material.

segments.text: (RAPPING) Six legs, eight legs, fly and crawl. Let's get it, world, come one, come all. Bugs can teach us so much more about the world. Let's go explore! Some of these facts are incredible knowing, like bees keep flowers and vegetables growing.

segments.text: The show wound up not using the song. But Adam couldn't stop listening to it. He walked around playing it over and over in his headphones.

segments.text: I mean, I knew she was skilled. But I sort of took it for granted. I was like, oh, that's just regular. Everybody can rhyme. Everybody I know can rhyme, you know? But I remember at that point being like, oh, you know what? This is really unique.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: Did this change your expectations for what this could be?

segments.speaker: Adam Mansbach
segments.text: Yeah, I think it opened-- it opened it up and made me want to maybe want to do more and see where we could take this.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: And so they did.

segments.speaker: Vivien
segments.text: Step into my office and have a seat.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: He and Vivien would plan out songs during the winters in California and record with his music industry friends back East during the summers. Writing for Vivien, Adam would layer in little in-jokes they shared or references that he knew his daughter would appreciate. Like when she was into Percy Jackson, he'd weave in the Greek gods. And when she was into Harry Potter, he worked that in.

segments.speaker: Adam Mansbach
segments.text: Yeah, I'm nice with my, like, Dumbledore, so what you want to rumble for?

segments.text: Vivien recorded under the moniker The Jazz Wolf, a name that she came up with. Her first real taste of mainstream exposure came by way of a song that Adam, who's originally from Massachusetts, wrote for her to perform in a hometown Boston accent.

segments.text: (RAPPING) My name's Clarissa, I'm wicked pissah. That girl Amber, I had to dis her. She opened up a powder keg. You're speaking chowderhead. I'm a hot target. You work at Star Market. Nobody [INAUDIBLE].

segments.text: They made a video for the song, which made it onto the home page of the popular humor website Funny or Die. But "Much Lobstah" was more like a comedy bit than a banger, more DJ Jazzy Jeff and the Fresh Prince than it was Eric B and Rakim. Adam didn't feel the song was representative of how he imagined Vivien as an artist.

segments.speaker: Adam Mansbach
segments.text: It was a funny song, but it was a funny song. It wasn't truly indicative of her skills as an emcee, because it was more focused on dropping Massachusetts-centric jokes.

segments.text: (RAPPING) Eat a grinder, drink a beer. Then I slap a critic. You're off the rails like Teddy was at Chappaquiddick. [BLAST]

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: Adam had told me that his kid rapped early on. But I didn't understand how serious the two of them were about this until September of 2017, when I received an email from Adam with no subject heading. Attached to the email were two remarkably well-produced songs, described in the body of the email simply as, Jazz Wolf Heat Rocks.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: One of these so-called Heat Rocks featured Vivien, who I had met once only briefly, but knew to be a small, blond White girl, rapping over a fluttery dancehall rhythm in full-on Jamaican patois.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: Did listening to this reggae song, penned by a best-selling Jewish author for his nine-year-old and most likely, recorded in or near his house on Martha's Vineyard, make me feel uncomfortable? Yeah, sure, a little. But I've been listening to hip hop a long time. And between all the sampling and biting and flipping styles, I've kind of made my peace with cultural appropriation. All I ask is that you give credit where credit is due and that you do your due diligence.

segments.speaker: Adam Mansbach
segments.text: You know, Neil, I should say that I had some misgivings about the song.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: [LAUGHING] I was going to ask.

segments.speaker: Adam Mansbach
segments.text: I definitely-- really, the first thing I did was send it to every Jamaican I knew.

segments.speaker: Adam Mansbach
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Adam Mansbach
segments.text: I'd be like, yo, so what do you think about this?

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: Anyway, the point is, it wasn't just me and some Caribbean Islanders who got this email. Adam was stepping up Vivien's game and had sent the Jazz Wolf de facto demo to just about every music industry contact he had. To a certain degree, it worked. Friends praised his daughter's music.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: Artists who Adam admired wanted to record with her. A big player in the music industry who had a hand in discovering Lauryn Hill suggested that they record more songs for a legitimate demo. Bolstered by all this interest, Adam set out to write Vivien something really special. It was the kind of thing he'd have written for himself back in his rapping days-- multi-syllabic, rapid fire, a real showpiece, designed to take the Jazz Wolf all the way to the next level. He was on a business trip, when the ghost writer in him really took over.

segments.speaker: Adam Mansbach
segments.text: And I remember I had to go away for a week. I was in Chicago, doing some stuff. And I writing bars for her. And I was really trying to write the most complicated, difficult verses I could. Because I knew she could handle it, and I was like, this is going to be really fun.

segments.speaker: Adam Mansbach
segments.text: And I came back with the song. And we rehearsed it for a long time. We got a beat from Dug Infinite, an illustrious producer, who worked with Common and all kinds of people. And Viv had been practicing it for weeks.

segments.speaker: Adam Mansbach
segments.text: And we had plans to go to his house and record it. She was nine at the time, I remember, because the chorus of the song played with the fact that she was nine. We flipped the chorus from nine millimeter goes bang. And it was like, wa da da dang, wa da da da dang. Hey, listen, 'cause I'm nine, and I kick enough slang.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: But despite all Adam's craft in preparation, there was an unforeseen, but not unforeseeable issue with the talent.

segments.speaker: Adam Mansbach
segments.text: She hadn't slept that night. I think we had a new baby. Viv has two younger sisters, and the older of the two at that time was only a few months old and was up, crying. And so Viv was on no sleep.

segments.speaker: Adam Mansbach
segments.text: And I remember we got to the studio really early. And she was just exhausted and not really at her peak. And it was difficult for her to get it down. And we kind of called it. We cut it short. I was like, you know what? Let's come back another day, Dug, because this isn't it.

segments.text: I'm sorry.

segments.text: [LAUGHING]

segments.text: No, I'm sorry. I didn't mean to be like that.

segments.speaker: Adam Mansbach
segments.text: Nah, are you kidding me? It's not your fault.

segments.text: That's Vivien. She was in the studio with her dad during this interview. She's 11 now.

segments.text: Right, so I remember coming back from there. And Viv was tired. And in the car, she told me. She was like, Papa, you know, I'm just not that into this right now, something along those lines. Like, I'm not into you writing me these rap songs right now.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: Vivian, do you remember this moment at all, this night?

segments.speaker: Vivien
segments.text: I did. And I think that the reason I told him then was that-- this is going to sound really stupid. But I thought that because-- I think he would be less angry if he knew I was tired and didn't want to argue.

segments.text: So you had already come to this decision?

segments.speaker: Vivien
segments.text: Yeah. I mean, we hadn't talked about it, but I'd already gone through it in my head what I was trying to say.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: OK, let's back up a bit. Vivien's dissatisfaction with how Adam was steeling her rap career goes back long before this night, back many car rides, in fact. She recalls trying to listen to new music while riding with her dad.

segments.speaker: Vivien
segments.text: Just flipping through radio stations in the car and him turning on a radio station, and I was like, oh yeah, this one. He's like, Oh, that's hot trash. We're not listening to that.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: You see, Adam didn't realize this, but even while she'd been sharing his love of hip hop, Vivien had been developing her own taste. She'd started to enjoy more contemporary music, God forbid, even pop music-- Taylor Swift, and later, Kesha and Nicki Minaj and Cardi B. But she'd been listening to music through Adam's ears long enough to understand and internalize just how much he wouldn't approve.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: So you felt like there were things that you liked that you couldn't tell him about?

segments.speaker: Vivien
segments.text: No. Well, there were things that I liked that I could tell him about, but that I didn't feel like there was any point to telling him about, because he would tell me all the errors. And run into where he keeps his records, and I'm like, oh, gosh.

segments.text: Do you remember any examples of this?

segments.speaker: Vivien
segments.text: Uh, one time, I was playing him a song from Hamilton, where someone was rapping really fast. And I played it, and he just half listened. And then afterward, he's like, you want to hear really fast rapping?

segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.text: At the risk of getting on my soapbox and with the full understanding, this is never going to make it actually into this piece, my thing with Hamilton was like, cool. Hamilton is fine. My issue with it is that a billion people who have no interest--

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: Here, Adam's critique of Hamilton, while spirited, is mostly remarkable, in that he somehow manages to vehemently object to the musical's popularity while simultaneously namedropping his friendship with one of its former stars, Daveed Diggs. Vivien didn't just want to feel free to listen to Hamilton in the car on the way to school. She wanted to incorporate all of her newfound influences into her own music.

segments.speaker: Vivien
segments.text: I felt like-- I mean, it's really cool that I'm doing all Papa's cool stuff. But if I have this voice, and I have access to this recording, can't I use it to do things that are more my style?

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: It's not all that surprising that someone Vivien's age would eventually diverge from the path her father set her on when she was six. And this wasn't even the first time Vivien had stood up to her dad. She's usually pretty outspoken. But she told me this time was different, that she had been more scared than usual to speak her mind and that it took her months to work up the courage.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: She was right to be concerned. Adam took it noticeably hard. To hear him tell it, he interpreted this slight rejection as a sort of referendum on his parenting.

segments.speaker: Adam Mansbach
segments.text: I felt a certain kind of sadness on a couple of levels-- first, disappointment in myself for getting carried away and making her feel uncomfortable or making her feel like an unwilling participant in this project. And also, just a sense of letdown that wow, maybe we were no longer going to be hanging out after dinner, playing instrumentals, and fitting rhymes to them, and practicing, and rehearsing, and cutting scratch demos, and that kind of thing. Because it was something that brought me a lot of joy, both reveling in her skill, but really more than anything, just spending time together, and that feeling of collaboration-- which is wonderful when you find it with anybody. But when you find it with your own kid, it's magical.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: I mean, this is me, like armchair psychotherapist. But was there any part of you that was deflecting some energy into this in a way that maybe was more for you than for Vivien?

segments.text: Five years-- I mean, that's a period of time that covers her mom and I splitting up. It covers a new relationship, two new babies. segments.text: I'm a father myself. It's a new thing, so new, In fact, that all I can say definitively about the experience so far is that I am terrified every single day about what's coming. I look around to my friends, as scared people do. And the thing that Adam pulled off gives me some hope.

segments.speaker: Neil Drumming
segments.text: He found an easy way to be with his daughter through difficult times. He constructed something fun that they could share, no matter what else was swirling around them. segments.text: Stop.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Neil Drumming.

segments.speaker: Starlee Kine
segments.text: I know a lot about small talk, because I worked in an office. And there's a lot of small talk that goes on. There's all these different forms of it. There's water cooler small talk, and there's elevator small talk, which actually isn't even that bad. Because most people think elevator small talk is the worst kind. But actually, I think it's OK, because it's finite. You know it's going to end at a certain point--

segments.speaker: Starlee Kine
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Starlee Kine
segments.text: --which I appreciate very much. And then there's even bathroom small talk where I work, which is the worst thing you're ever going to experience in your entire life.

segments.speaker: Starlee Kine
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Starlee Kine
segments.text: They'll be people small-talking through the stalls. I actually have some audio of small talk to play for you.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Coffee is on its way. Here is a special selection of the Viking blend. And I have to get back to work.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Starlee Kine
segments.text: So that's what happened in my office. Almost every day, that seems to happen, actually. We know we're drinking coffee. It's being made. But for some reason, when you do small talk, when you're caught in the trap of small talk, you feel you just had to talk about what's immediately happening in front of you, even though it's so obvious. And it's not even his fault. You know what I mean? It just-- everyone does it.

segments.speaker: Starlee Kine
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Starlee Kine
segments.text: And so I can't take it anymore. So I devised The Rundown to eliminate small talk forever from the world. I want it to be done with. The Rundown is what it's supposed to do. The goal Of the Rundown is it's supposed to turn conversations from the conversations you're supposed to be having to the conversations you want to be having. OK?

segments.speaker: Starlee Kine
segments.text: And so I also have an example of The Rundown. I went to a movie. And there was a ticket guy selling tickets. And I just started talking to him. So it can be done on anyone.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: I had ramen noodles for breakfast.

segments.speaker: Starlee Kine
segments.text: The $0.25 ones or did you pay-- or the fancy ones?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: I didn't pay for them. My girlfriend bought them.

segments.speaker: Starlee Kine
segments.text: OK, and so you're thinking small talk. You're going to go after the ramen noodles, right? Like, what kind of ramen noodles? What hot water, meat? Something like that-- but if you're doing The Rundown, you just seize on the most interesting part of the conversation, OK?

segments.speaker: Starlee Kine
segments.text: And so he did give me a very, very valuable clue. He gave me this girlfriend, wonderful girlfriend, character to work with, OK? From that, you can proceed to--

segments.speaker: Starlee Kine
segments.text: Are you in love?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: I love her.

segments.speaker: Starlee Kine
segments.text: We don't know if-- you're not in love?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Oh, well, I think, yeah. I am definitely in love.

segments.speaker: Starlee Kine
segments.text: OK, so that's a little bit more to go with, right? Now we know he's capable of love--

segments.speaker: Starlee Kine
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Starlee Kine
segments.text: --which is a lot more than knowing that he just had ramen noodles, right? And from there, OK, the possibilities just open up wide. You can pretty much go for anything now. So then you just keep going.

segments.speaker: Starlee Kine
segments.text: How many one-night stands have you had?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Uh, well, I don't-- I know how many girls I've been with, but I don't-- I never really counted which of them are one-night stands exactly.

segments.speaker: Starlee Kine
segments.text: How many girls?

segments.speaker: Starlee Kine
segments.text: 44 and 1/2. How many virgins?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: I don't know. Estimate-- roughly, probably four or five.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Starlee Kine
segments.text: OK, so you might think, how many virgins, is an inappropriate question. But I actually think it's the perfect fallback, if you have nothing else to ask. You know what I mean? Because--

segments.speaker: Starlee Kine
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Starlee Kine
segments.text: --as you can see, it's totally OK. He doesn't mind telling you. People are just wait-- they love to talk about themselves, you know? And that's what people want. And they also like to be asked questions that they have answers for. He completely knows the answer to, how many virgins?

segments.speaker: Starlee Kine
segments.text: So then they feel good about themselves. And they'll keep going. And from there, it's pretty smooth sailing.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: The first one that came along was for 2 and 1/2 years.

segments.speaker: Starlee Kine
segments.text: Really?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: That was the first girl I was ever with, though.

segments.speaker: Starlee Kine
segments.text: That was?

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: She was a virgin, too. We were both virgins. It was good, you know, but it was weird. It was kind of like an all day, all-around-town sort of thing. Because it started at her grandparents' house, which is in this all yellow room. The sheets were yellow. The window curtains were yellow.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: And then it just wasn't working out. So then we drove out to this spot by a drive-in movie screen that was abandoned. But it was a good experience altogether. I enjoyed it.

segments.speaker: Starlee Kine
segments.text: So that was a minute and 26 seconds. And now, after a minute and 26, through The Rundown, I know what he's had for breakfast, that he's capable of love, how many girls he slept with, how many of them were virgins, who he lost his-- first lost his virginity to, and even the color wallpaper of her grandmother's house. So that's pretty good. That's a pretty successful Rundown.

segments.speaker: Starlee Kine
segments.text: And there's a few simple rules for everyone to be able to do it just like this eventually. So the first rule is, number one, small talk is a conversation you're supposed to be having. And The Rundown is a conversation you want to be having. Right?

segments.speaker: Starlee Kine
segments.text: Number two is, why chew the fat, when you can chew the meat? OK?

segments.speaker: Starlee Kine
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Starlee Kine
segments.text: Also very important. Number three is, if you can think it, you can ask it.

segments.speaker: Starlee Kine
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Starlee Kine
segments.text: OK? And then, if all else fails, or even if all else doesn't fail, number four is, how many virgins?

segments.speaker: Starlee Kine
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Starlee Kine
segments.text: So that's the run down.
